package.name: Path
package.description: Native operating-system strings and filesystem paths

modules.name: OsString
modules.header:
Text as the operating system stores it, kept lossless.
A filename is not text. On the Unix systems it is bytes with two exclusions — no slash, no NUL — and nothing
obliges those bytes to be UTF-8. On Windows it is UTF-16 code units, and nothing obliges them to pair: names
with unpaired surrogates exist on real disks. A path type built on `String` would refuse those names, and a
program that cannot open a file because of its name is wrong in the way that loses data.
So the native string stores exactly what the system does — bytes there, code units here — behind one alias,
and the conversions are asymmetric on purpose: UTF-8 in always succeeds, since valid text encodes into either
representation; UTF-8 out is fallible, since the system's names are under no obligation to be text at all.

modules.name: Parts
modules.header:
The named parts of a path, and the joins and simplifications that stay lexical.
Everything here reads units and produces views into them or fresh buffers from them; nothing asks the
filesystem anything. That matters most for `Normalize`: it resolves `..` by dropping the segment before it,
which is the truth about directories and a lie about symbolic links — `a/link/..` need not be `a` when `link`
points elsewhere. The lie is documented, deliberate, and cheap; the truth costs a filesystem and arrives with
canonicalization in the S tasks.

modules.name: Path
modules.header:
A path is a name with structure: segments, separated.
`Path` borrows and `PathBuffer` owns, exactly as `OsStringView` and `OsString` do underneath them — a path adds
meaning, not storage. The meaning is small and lexical: which units separate segments, and how to walk the
segments between them. Nothing here touches a filesystem; whether a path names anything real is a question for
the S tasks, asked through the system.
Windows accepts both slashes and prefers the backslash; the Unix systems know only the forward one. That pair of
facts is the whole platform difference at this layer, and it is confined to two functions.

modules.name: PathBuffer
modules.header:
A path that owns its units and can grow.
The growable operation a path needs is exactly one: push a segment, with a separator supplied where one is
missing. Everything else — parent, filename, joins that produce fresh paths — reads structure and lives with
it; the buffer is where segments accumulate on the way to a system call.

modules.name: Prefix
modules.header:
What stands before a path's first real segment.
The Unix systems have one answer: nothing, or the root. Windows has a family — a drive (`C:`), a UNC share
(`\server\share`), and the verbatim prefix (`\?\`) that turns parsing off for everything after it — and which
one a path carries changes what "absolute" means for it. `C:name` is neither relative nor absolute but
drive-relative, a shape only Windows has.
Nothing here folds case. `C:` and `c:` are the same drive to the filesystem and different units to this layer,
exactly as two names differing in case are: which spellings the system treats as one is the system's opinion,
and a path library that imitates it bakes today's opinion into tomorrow's comparison.

modules.name: Presentation
modules.header:
Showing a name the system may not have written in text, without pretending either that it is text or that it
is not.
A native name is bytes on the Unix systems and UTF-16 code units on Windows, and neither is obliged to be valid.
Real disks hold names that are not text: a byte sequence that is not UTF-8, a code unit with no partner. That is
why `OsString` exists and why converting out of it is fallible. But a program still has to say something when it
reports which file it could not open, and refusing to render the name is not an answer a user can act on.
So the two protocols answer two different questions and neither one compromises. `Display` is the name as a
reader should see it: every unit that is not text becomes U+FFFD, the replacement character, which is exactly
what the substitution is for. It is lossy and says so; it is for a message, never for reopening the file.
`Debug` is the name as it actually is: every native unit survives, with the ones that are not text spelled as
escapes, so two different names never render alike. The exact conversions in `OsStringView::ToText` and the
filesystem operations are untouched by either — a path still travels to a system call as the units it is.
One rule follows from that and is worth stating: a precision is refused rather than applied. Truncating a path
produces a different path, and one that may well exist; a rendering that silently answers about another file is
worse than a rendering that refuses.

doc.summary: This native text as UTF-8, or nothing where it is not text.
doc.markdown:
This native text as UTF-8, or nothing where it is not text.
The fallible direction, and fallible for a different reason per platform: Unix bytes may simply not be
UTF-8, and Windows units may hold an unpaired surrogate, which no UTF-8 sequence can spell. It fails with
`InvalidUtf8` for both, because both mean the same thing to the caller — this name is not text, and a
program that must show it anyway shows it lossily by its own policy, knowingly.
doc.returns: the units converted to text, or a failure when they are not valid in it

doc.summary: Writes the name as text, with every native unit that is not text replaced by U+FFFD.
doc.markdown:
Writes the name as text, with every native unit that is not text replaced by U+FFFD.
Lossy, deliberately and only here. A name the system holds is not obliged to be text, and a program
reporting which file it could not open still has to name it; U+FFFD is what the standard provides for
exactly that. What this produces is for a reader, never for reopening the file — two different names can
render alike, and `Debug` is the rendering that does not.
Reports whatever the writer reported, and `UnsupportedRequest` for any style or precision. A precision is
refused rather than applied because a truncated path is a different path, and may be one that exists.
doc.returns: success when the whole name was accepted

doc.summary: Writes the name exactly, quoted, with every unit that is not text spelled as an escape.
doc.markdown:
Writes the name exactly, quoted, with every unit that is not text spelled as an escape.
Nothing is lost: a Unix byte outside a well-formed sequence is written `\x{nn}` and a Windows code unit
with no partner is written `\u{xxxx}`, so the native units can be read back off the output and two
different names never render alike. The quote, the backslash and the control characters are escaped the way
this repository escapes them everywhere else.
Reports whatever the writer reported, and `UnsupportedRequest` for any style or precision.
doc.returns: success when the whole name was accepted

`a//b/` walks as `a`, `b`. A leading separator is the root, which the walk reports as an empty first component
so that an absolute path is distinguishable from a relative one holding the same segments.

items.name: Normalize
items.signature: pub func Normalize(allocator: Allocator, path: Path) -> PathBuffer ! TextError

doc.summary:
A fresh buffer holding `path` lexically simplified: separator runs collapsed to the preferred separator, `.`
segments dropped, and `..` resolved against the segment before it.
doc.markdown:
A fresh buffer holding `path` lexically simplified: separator runs collapsed to the preferred separator, `.`
segments dropped, and `..` resolved against the segment before it.
Lexically is the load-bearing word. Dropping `x/..` is the truth about directories and a lie about symbolic
links — `a/link/..` need not be `a` when `link` points elsewhere — so this is for display, comparison and
deduplication, and the filesystem-true answer is canonicalization, which asks the system. A `..` with nothing
before it survives in a relative path and vanishes at the root, where there is nowhere further up.
doc.returns: the path with its redundant components resolved, or why it could not be

On the Unix systems, rooted is absolute. On Windows a rooted drive (`C:\x`), a share and a verbatim path are
absolute; `C:name` is drive-relative and `\name` drive-absent, and neither names one place on its own.
